name: Volcanic ash

lead: Ground volcanic ash and related volcanic minerals appear in some Korean-origin masks and cleansers as oil-absorbing ingredients. People with oily skin use them for less shine, cleaner-feeling pores and a matte, clearer look.

The chain is absorption: the fine mineral particles take up surface sebum, so skin looks less shiny and pores look less clogged. Users and marketing describe this effect; no study of cosmetic volcanic ash on human skin was identified, and the literature found covers volcanology and exposure hazards.

paras: Used as a wash-off mask or cleanser, typically applied to the oily zones for several minutes once or twice a week, then rinsed and followed by moisturiser. It is often combined with other clay or charcoal products. Matte results are visible right after rinsing.
Raw eruption ash is abrasive and can irritate eyes, skin and airways. Cosmetic safety data were not found, and drying or over-cleansing can irritate skin.

angle.text: Volcanic ash appears in some K-beauty masks and cleansers, used to absorb oil and leave oily skin looking matte. The fine mineral particles take up surface sebum, which means less shine and cleaner-looking pores.

lead: Volcanic ash is fine fragmented rock, mineral crystal and volcanic glass, under 2 mm in diameter, produced by explosive eruptions.[1][2] Its chemistry varies with the magma type, from silica-poor basaltic to silica-rich rhyolitic ash.[1]

In skincare, ground volcanic ash, volcanic clay and related volcanic minerals are used in some products, particularly Korean-origin masks and cleansers, as sebum-absorbing ingredients. The sources reviewed for this article describe the material in geological and health-hazard terms and do not document cosmetic use; no study of cosmetic volcanic ash on human skin was identified.
infobox: Glass shards, mineral crystals, rock fragments[1]

paras: Volcanic ash consists of angular glass shards, crystals such as quartz, feldspar and pyroxene, and rock fragments. It is hard, abrasive and insoluble in water.[2][1] Fresh ash can carry soluble salts including chloride, sulfate and fluoride compounds that make it acidic when moist.[1]

Volcanology references describe inhaled ash as causing respiratory, eye and skin irritation, mostly short-term; prolonged exposure to silica-rich ash carries a theoretical silicosis risk, though Wikipedia notes no documented silicosis cases from volcanic ash.[1] These accounts concern eruption exposure, not processed cosmetic ingredients.

No studies found. Related literature concerns particulate toxicity in general: a review of nanomaterials discusses human exposure to natural particles such as volcanic ash,[3] and laboratory studies of air-pollution particles examine inflammatory responses in lung cells;[4] these are not studies of cosmetic use.
